Letter to the Editor
Utility of ultrasonography in evaluating
muscle contractions in stiff-person
syndrome
Keywords:
Stiff-person syndrome
Ultrasonography
Muscle contractionsDear Editor,
1. Introduction
Stiff-person syndrome (SPS) is a rare disorder characterized by pro-
gressive muscle stiffness, rigidity, and painful spasms[1]. The diagnosis
of SPS is established using electromyography; muscle stiffness and ri-
gidity arise as a consequence of continuous involuntary motor unit ac-
tivity in agonist and antagonist axial and proximal limb muscles [2].
We observed involuntary muscle contractions using ultrasonography
and evaluated the distribution pattern in a patient with SPS.
2. Case report
A 27-year-old, right handed, Japanese woman presented with con-
tinuous bilateral severe pain in the lower limbs, followed by chronic
widespread pain. At the age of 31, she began experiencing widespread
muscle cramps and twitches in the lower limbs. At the age of 33, she de-
veloped muscular weakness and had dif ���culty in walking and
swallowing. She then visited Juntendo hospital. She reported strong,
painful muscle twitches and cramps and an extreme degree of muscle
stiffness and rigidity in the lower limbs, resulting in limited range of
motion in the knee and ankle joints. We continuously observed co-
contracting agonist and antagonist muscles in the upper and lower
limbs and a wide-based gait. She exhibited grip myotonia-like move-
ments, and postural tremor was observed in both hands. The patient's
grip strength was 9 kg in both hands, and deep tendon re���exes revealed
hyperre���exia. Using a numerical rating scale of pain the patient report-
ed: 80/100; widespread pain: 12/19; and her severity score: 5/12 [3].
Motor symptoms were evaluated using the Barthel Index (85/100).
We measured the “distribution of stiffness ” throughout her body, as
previously described [4]. She presented autonomic dysfunction, which
included pollakiuria, constipation, diarrhea, and hyperhidrosis. Photo-
phobia and dilated pupils (6 mm/6 mm) were also detected. Serum an-
tibody examinations were negative for anti-IgG VGKC antibody
[14.6 pM ( b72 pM)] and anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) 65
antibody. Anti-amphiphysin antibody was also negative (Euroimmun,
Luebeck, Germany). The total calcium concentration in her peripheral
blood was 9.0 mg/dl (8.8–10.6 mg/dl). Brain and spinal magnetic reso-
nance imaging did not show any abnormalities. Chest and abdominal
CT scan did not reveal any mass lesions. We performed surface EMG
using Bagnoli-16® (Delsys, Natick, MA, USA). Surface EMG revealed
continuous motor unit activity and 8-Hz grouped discharge with
waxing–waning in both agonist and antagonist muscles in the same
phase (Supplementary Fig. S1 (a) and (b)). Needle EMG revealed 8 –
10-Hz grouped discharges comprising multiple motor units. We did
not observe myokymic discharges, ���brillation potentials, fasciculation
potentials, positive-sharp waves and there was a full EMG interference
pattern. Therefore, based on these results and clinical features, the pa-
tient was diagnosed with SPS, thereby con ���rming the results of previ-
ous reports [1]. On admission, she initially received pulse steroid
ly. However, her symptoms did not improve. We assessed her muscle
contractions using ultrasonography for each of the muscle points ( Fig.
1, Table S1, and supplementary material and methods). Detailed
methods for ultrasonography have been described elsewhere [5].
Using ultrasonography, we observed persistent continuous and invol-
untary muscle contractions, without voluntary movements in the
upper and lower limbs (Video S1). These muscle contractions were
widespread at rest (independently con���rmed by more than two clini-
cians) and we therefore concluded that they were involuntary. To quan-
tify our observations we counted the number of muscle contractions
over a 10 s interval in each muscle (Table S1). After evaluation, we ad-
ditionally administered a second round of steroid pulse therapy at
1000 mg/day for 3 days and ���ve sessions of plasma exchange. We
then prescribed a 30-mg/day dose of prednisolone, which was later re-
duced to 5 mg/month. One month after admission we assessed her mus-
cle contractions using ultrasonography and surface EMG, which
revealed a reduced number of muscle contractions and recovery of re-
ciprocal movements in both her lower limbs (Fig. 1 and Supplementary
Fig. S1(c)). She was then discharged from our hospital. Three months
later, she was re-admitted because of exacerbation of muscle stiffness
and painful spasms. A one-time dose of intravenous immunoglobulin
was administered (0.4 g/kg for 5 days; kg, body weight). We then pre-
scribed dantrolene (75 mg/day) and baclofen (15 mg/day). Her condi-
and 3 mg/day tizanidine for internal use. After treatment, her symptoms
partially improved. Under ultrasonographic observation, the total
counts of muscle contractions decreased from 90 to 36, with improve-
ments in her numerical rating scale of pain score (Fig. 1 and Video S1).
3. Discussion
Objective measures of therapeutic ef���cacy in the short-term in indi-
vidual patients are of increasing interest in neurological disorders, par-
ticularly those where the therapy used is high-risk, and clinical
measures of ef ���cacy are either insensitive or where because of

signi���cant associated psychiatric disease, as is the case in SPS [1],r e l i -
able clinical assessment is dif���cult. We have provided preliminary evi-
dence that muscle ultrasonography, which is non-invasive and
painless, is a potential method of quantifying subclinical therapeutic re-
sponse in SPS.
In our patient the most symptomatic muscles were the quadriceps
femoris muscles bilaterally. Interestingly, whilst ultrasound con���rmed
that the strongest muscle contractions were also in quadriceps femoris,
we also observed more widespread muscle contractions, mainly in ap-
pendicular muscles and less frequently in axial muscles. Our observa-
tion that muscle contractions can be detected reproducibly using
ultrasound in widespread, clinically unaffected muscles would indicate
that such contractions are involuntary. Moreover, the observation that
the same contractions are associated with 8–10 Hz grouped discharges
on simultaneous needle EMG would indicate that the involuntary mus-
cle contractions are generated centrally.
After undergoing comprehensive treatment, the muscle
contractions partially improved and clinical symptoms were ameliorat-
ed. The degree of involuntary muscle contractions observed
ultrasonographically seemed to correspond with the patient's level of
clinical severity. To the best of our knowledge, there are no reports re-
garding the quantitative assessment of muscle contractions using ultra-
sonography for in patients with SPS. Ultrasonography may be a
supportive tool to help establish the diagnosis and severity of SPS, and
to quantify response to therapy.
In conclusion, further studies with more patients are required to
con���rm our ���ndings of aberrant involuntary muscle contractions
using ultrasonography.

We performed surface EMG using Bagnoli-16® (Delsys, Natick, MA, USA). Surface EMG revealed continuous motor unit activity and 8-Hz grouped discharge with waxing–waning in both agonist and antagonist muscles in the same phase (Supplementary Fig. S1 (a) and (b)). Needle EMG revealed 8 – 10-Hz grouped discharges comprising multiple motor units. We did not observe myokymic discharges, fibrillation potentials, fasciculation potentials, positive-sharp waves and there was a full EMG interference pattern.

On admission, she initially received pulse steroid ly. However, her symptoms did not improve. We assessed her muscle contractions using ultrasonography for each of the muscle points ( Fig. 1, Table S1, and supplementary material and methods). Detailed methods for ultrasonography have been described elsewhere [5]. Using ultrasonography, we observed persistent continuous and involuntary muscle contractions, without voluntary movements in the upper and lower limbs (Video S1). These muscle contractions were widespread at rest (independently confirmed by more than two clinicians) and we therefore concluded that they were involuntary. To quantify our observations we counted the number of muscle contractions over a 10 s interval in each muscle (Table S1). After evaluation, we additionally administered a second round of steroid pulse therapy at 1000 mg/day for 3 days and five sessions of plasma exchange. We then prescribed a 30-mg/day dose of prednisolone, which was later reduced to 5 mg/month. One month after admission we assessed her muscle contractions using ultrasonography and surface EMG, which revealed a reduced number of muscle contractions and recovery of reciprocal movements in both her lower limbs (Fig. 1 and Supplementary Fig. S1(c)). She was then discharged from our hospital. Three months later, she was re-admitted because of exacerbation of muscle stiffness and painful spasms. A one-time dose of intravenous immunoglobulin was administered (0.4 g/kg for 5 days; kg, body weight). We then prescribed dantrolene (75 mg/day) and baclofen (15 mg/day). Her condition and 3 mg/day tizanidine for internal use. After treatment, her symptoms partially improved. Under ultrasonographic observation, the total counts of muscle contractions decreased from 90 to 36, with improvements in her numerical rating scale of pain score (Fig. 1 and Video S1).
